title: Commas Before Joining Words
keyIdea: A compound sentence is two complete sentences (independent clauses) joined by a coordinating conjunction: and, but, or, so or yet. Put a comma just before the joining word: “I wanted to go outside, but it was raining.” To test it, cover the joining word and read each half. If both halves have their own subject and verb and make sense alone, use the comma. If the second half has no subject of its own, as in “She sang and danced”, it is one sentence with two verbs, so there is no comma. A comma on its own, with no joining word, cannot join two sentences.
familyTip: Read a page of your child's writing together and hunt for and, but and so. For each one, cover it with a finger and ask: could both halves be sentences on their own? If yes, pop a comma in front. If one half has no who, leave it.

visual.caption: Comma before the joining word, or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The rain stopped and we went out.
I was hungry so I ate a pear.
Max can swim or ride a bike.
We ran fast but we missed the bus.
Jo picked up the cup and drank.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: cover each half to test it, tap the gap for the comma, pick the joining word that fits, edit a paragraph, and find which and joins two sentences.

kid: And, but, or, so and yet are joining words. They can join two whole sentences into one long one. We call that a compound sentence.
When a joining word links two whole sentences, put a comma just before it. For example: The bus was late, so we walked. Both halves make sense on their own.
Here is the test. Cover the joining word with your finger. Read each half. Does each half have its own who and its own doing word? Then add the comma.

Sometimes the second half has no who. In Mia sang and danced, Mia does both things. That is one sentence, so there is no comma. The comma goes before the joining word, never after it, and a comma alone is not enough.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. In the US this is Common Core L.4.2c (use a comma before a coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence) and builds towards L.5.2 and L.7.1b. In England, Year 2 pupils learn coordination with and, or and but, and Years 3 to 6 extend this to compound sentences and commas used to clarify meaning.

A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). The comma goes before the conjunction. A simple sentence with a compound predicate (one subject, two verbs: “Leo opened the box and laughed”) takes no comma, because the second part cannot stand alone.

Usage note: many style guides allow the comma to be left out when both clauses are very short and the meaning is clear (“I came and I saw”), and British writers drop it more often than American ones. Pupils are taught to use it, and US tests expect it, so the lesson treats it as the rule.

Common mistakes: putting a comma before every and, including in compound predicates and lists of two; putting the comma after the conjunction; using a comma with no conjunction (a comma splice); and treating and in a phrase such as fish and chips as if it joined two sentences. The lab practises each of these checks.

practice.prompt: Which sentence needs a comma before the joining word?
choices: The sun set and the stars came out.
The cat yawned and stretched.
Ella read and wrote all morning.
practice.hint: Cover and. Which sentence has a whole sentence on both sides?
practice.explain: The stars came out stands alone, so it is a compound sentence: The sun set, and the stars came out. The other two have one who doing two things.

practice.prompt: Raj has {n} sweets. Where does the comma go: “Raj had {n} sweets so he shared them”?
choices: after sweets, before so
after so
after Raj
practice.hint: The comma goes where the two sentences meet.
practice.explain: Raj had {n} sweets is one sentence and he shared them is another. The comma goes just before so: Raj had {n} sweets, so he shared them.

choices: Ben ran to the door and opened it.
Ben ran to the door, and opened it.
Ben ran to the door and, opened it.
practice.hint: Does opened it have its own who?
practice.explain: Opened it has no who of its own, because Ben does both things. That is one sentence with two verbs, so no comma.

practice.prompt: The class read {n} pages. Which joining word fits: “We read {n} pages, ___ we still had more to go”?
choices: but
so
or
practice.hint: Do the two halves agree, or is there a contrast?
practice.explain: Reading {n} pages and still having more to go is a contrast, so but fits. So would mean a result, and or would mean a choice.

practice.prompt: Which sentence has a comma splice?
choices: It was late, we went to bed.
It was late, so we went to bed.
It was late so we went to bed.
practice.hint: Look for two sentences joined by a comma with no joining word.
practice.explain: It was late, we went to bed joins two sentences with only a comma. That is a comma splice. Add so after the comma to fix it.

choices: two complete sentences joined by a word like and, but or so
a sentence with a list in it
a sentence that asks a question
pool.hint: Think about what the joining word links.
pool.explain: A compound sentence joins two complete sentences (independent clauses) with a coordinating conjunction, such as and, but, or, so or yet.

pool.prompt: Lily swam {n} lengths. Which version puts the comma in the right place?
choices: Lily swam {n} lengths, but the water was cold.
Lily swam {n} lengths but, the water was cold.
Lily swam, {n} lengths but the water was cold.
pool.hint: Where do the two sentences meet?
pool.explain: Both halves stand alone, so the comma goes just before but. Not after it, and not inside one half.

pool.prompt: Why does “Zara laughed and clapped” have no comma?
choices: Clapped has no who of its own, so it is one sentence
And never takes a comma
The sentence is too short
pool.hint: Cover and. Can clapped be a sentence on its own?
pool.explain: Zara does both things, so laughed and clapped share one subject. That is a compound predicate, so there is no comma.

pool.prompt: The team scored {n} goals. Which joining word fits: “We scored {n} goals, ___ we won the cup”?
choices: so
or
but
pool.hint: Is the second half a result of the first?
pool.explain: Winning the cup is a result of scoring {n} goals, so so fits. But shows a contrast and or gives a choice.

pool.prompt: Which and joins two sentences: “Ali and Sam went out and Sam fell over”?
choices: the second and
the first and
neither and
pool.hint: Which and has a whole sentence after it?
pool.explain: Ali and Sam is two names. Sam fell over is a whole sentence, so the comma goes before the second and.

pool.prompt: How do you fix “The phone rang, nobody answered”?
choices: add but after the comma
take the comma out
add a comma after nobody
pool.hint: A comma alone cannot join two sentences.
pool.explain: This is a comma splice. Keep the comma and add a joining word: The phone rang, but nobody answered.

choices: Grandma knitted a hat and gave it to me.
Grandma knitted a hat and I wore it.
Grandma was tired yet she kept going.
pool.hint: Which one has only one who?
pool.explain: Grandma knitted and gave: one who, two verbs, so no comma. The other two join two whole sentences.

pool.prompt: Which sentence uses the comma correctly?
choices: You can paint, or you can draw.
You can paint or, you can draw.
You can paint or you, can draw.
pool.hint: Find where the two sentences meet.
pool.explain: You can paint and you can draw are both sentences. The comma goes just before or.
